The '''Vesperan Language''' was the principal language of the [[Vesperan Kingdom]] and later the official administrative, legal, military, diplomatic, and ceremonial language of the [[Vesperan Empire]]. It developed from older western dialects into an imperial standard written in the [[Vesperan Alphabet]].

Vesperan mattered because it was one of the empire's main tools of rule. It connected the court at [[Vespera]], provincial ministries, military commands, legal records, religious ceremony, and occupied territories to a single imperial administrative culture.

== Development ==

Source material traces Old Vesperan to western dialects that began consolidating around the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Early written forms were associated with religious texts, royal decrees, trade records, and court administration.

By the later kingdom period, Vesperan had become a language of government rather than only a regional speech. The [[Royal Language Decree of 1652]] established a standardized classical form for law, administration, court use, and official recordkeeping.

== Imperial Standard ==

After the [[Imperial Proclamation of 1710]], Vesperan became the imperial language of a much larger state. The [[Imperial Language Academy]], established in source material in 1715, supervised official grammar, administrative vocabulary, spelling standards, translation practice, and the use of Vesperan in provincial government.

The language carried the empire's political vocabulary. Terms for hierarchy, military service, taxation, religious loyalty, legal status, and imperial citizenship spread through territories controlled or influenced by Vespera.

== Cultural And Political Role ==

Vesperan was used by the imperial court, the [[Imperial Council]], military commands, provincial administrations, state schools, diplomatic missions, and major religious institutions of the [[Imperial Cult]]. In the capital, institutions such as the [[University of Vespera]] and [[Vesperan Historical Institute]] helped preserve older texts and produce official scholarship.

In conquered areas, Vesperan language policy could be coercive. Occupation administrations promoted or required Vesperan in schools, courts, government offices, and cultural institutions. This made the language a practical tool of administration and a symbol of imperial control.

The same policy strengthened resistance identities in some places. [[Belcantese Language|Belcantese]] and [[Veszpremi Language|Veszpremi]] sources describe local languages as markers of defiance under Vesperan pressure.

== Collapse And Legacy ==

Vesperan ceased to be the language of a functioning imperial state when the [[Vesperan Empire]] collapsed in 1949. The source language page extends the language era to 1951, which may reflect the [[Continuation War]] and continued use by loyalist commands rather than recognized state authority.

After 1949, Vesperan survived in archives, scholarship, legal terminology, ceremonial quotations, place names, former military vocabulary, and cultural preservation work. Its status after the empire's collapse varied by region: some successor states preserved it as a scholarly language, while former occupied peoples treated it as a reminder of imperial rule.

== Canon Notes ==

The extracted source gives a broad 1200-1951 language era but also identifies 1650-1949 as the official state period. This draft treats 1949 as the end of state language authority and 1951 as possible residual loyalist or Continuation War usage.

The source also conflicts on the size of the alphabet: the language page describes a 28-letter alphabet, while the alphabet page describes a 32-letter system. The current draft keeps that as an open orthographic issue rather than choosing one silently.
